subject: clockworkDog
pitch: A wind-up clockwork terrier made of polished brass and copper. Riveted body plates, visible gears turning in its chest, a big winding key on its back, springy jointed legs, floppy leather ears, glass-lens eyes with a green tint, a tail made of a coiled spring, and a little red collar with a brass tag.
reasoning:
I'm planning the module structure for a clockwork terrier model, setting the scale for body length and shoulder height with the model facing forward, and sketching out the joint hierarchy starting from a root hip joint.

I'm working through the leg chains, using four-joint chains (shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw) built from polyline paths for each leg, and making sure to specify explicit parent joints so they attach correctly to the spine rather than relying on nearest-joint defaults. Now I'm considering how to build the floppy ears, likely using a slab or membrane shape between two points.

For the gears visible through the chest plate, I'm planning cylinder geometry for the gear body and a ring of small boxes stuck radially outward to form teeth, using a ring frame helper so each tooth aligns outward with proper orientation and embed depth.

For the tail, I'm working out a coiled spring shape using a spiral path swept into a tube, then chaining it into joints so the tail can bend segment by segment, pulling a handful of knots from the spiral for the chain's bone structure.

Now I'm figuring out the spiral's geometry: where to center it at the rear, what radius and axis to give it so the coil tilts up and back like a stylized spring tail, and tuning the pitch and turn count so it rises a reasonable amount without being too long or short.

Then I shift to the body itself, planning a smooth loft between stations from rump to chest, with a mottled brass/copper paint for a patinaed metal look, and figuring out how to scatter small rivet spheres across the surface of that loft.

For rivet placement I work out a nearest-surface-point approach: casting from offset points near the body to find the closest hit on the surface, which gives both position and normal for embedding the rivet spheres correctly on the sides, then grouping these into rows to suggest riveted plate seams.

For legs I'm planning the joint chain: shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw positioned downward to the ground, so I can sweep a tube along this polyline to form the limb and attach a sole mesh at the tip.

Now I'm working out the hind leg geometry similarly, with hip, stifle, hock, and toe points forming a plausible digitigrade bend, and naming each joint uniquely so the chains don't collide across front and back legs.

Then I'm setting up the spine, neck, and head chain: a short neck path from chest to head base, with the final joint acting as the head anchor, and building the skull as a lofted shape tapering from a wider base near the neck down to a narrower snout tip.

For the head details, I'm adding small spherical eyes tinted a soft green near the front of the skull, and planning leather-brown ear slabs hanging from the back of the head, shaped by a few control points.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry itself — thin flat prisms positioned sideways on either side of the head, using the same point-based slab approach. Then I'm sketching a winding key on the back of the body, a small cylinder with a torus handle on top.

I'm roughing out the body's cross-section stations (rump, hip, mid, chest) with their widths and heights to get a chunky terrier-like proportions, checking leg length against ground clearance, then placing the key shaft at the hip station's top point.

For the winding key itself, I'm sizing a cylinder shaft and topping it with a torus rotated flat to form the loop handle. For the chest decoration, I'm planning to stick a brass disc flush against the chest's front surface and ring it with small copper teeth to suggest a gear mechanism.

Then I'm thinking through adding rows of rivets along the body sides by finding nearest surface points at varying heights and depths, placing small spheres embedded into the shell—reusing the same sphere geometry across rivets should keep things efficient within the mesh part limits.

I'm also considering stuck-on plate panels for a riveted-metal look: thin boxes aligned to the surface normal at a few side locations, oriented so the box's tangent faces follow the body curvature. For coloring, I'm leaning toward a mottled brass paint for the main body and a coppery tone for accent plates.

Now I'm figuring out the leather/collar details — a red torus loop around the neck tilted to match posture, with a small brass cylinder tag hanging at the throat. I'm sketching neck joint placement and bone assignment to anchor the collar and tag correctly to the neck chain.

For the head, I'm lofting the skull and muzzle shape through stations tapering toward the nose tip, adding a small black sphere nose at the end, and positioning side-mounted eye spheres (green glass with a brass bezel) symmetrically on the head width.

For the legs, I'm setting up four joint chains with role "leg" and naming conventions for shoulder/elbow/wrist/paw on front legs and hip/knee/hock/toe on hind legs, then sweeping tapered copper tubes along each chain to form the limbs.

For feet, I'm placing small boxes at the paw tips but need to make sure the joint sits right at floor level (y=0) so the leg tubes don't dip below the ground plane given their radius.

Now I'm designing the leg chain generator with named joints for front legs (shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw) and hind legs (hip, knee, hock, paw) using mirrored x-coordinates for left/right sides, making sure the hind legs have the digitigrade bend pattern with the hock angled back and toe forward. I'm checking that each chain's joint-name array matches the number of path segments plus one, and that the polyline paths feed in as arrays of coordinate triples for the chain builder to consume correctly.

I'm now thinking through the body rig structure—deciding whether to use a single root "body" joint or add a spine chain connecting hips to chest, considering how the first joint of the chain should inherit its parent from the root joint.

I'm working out the leg attachment points along the spine — front legs parenting to "spine2" near the mid-spine joint, hind legs parenting to "hips" — and checking the knot positions from the polyline to confirm where each spine joint lands. Now I'm starting on the body loft, setting up stations along the spine curve for the sweep.

Defining body and head stations...

For the head, I'll reuse the same brass mottle paint for consistency, placing the skull-brow-muzzle-nose loft on the "head" bone with a dark sphere for the nose tip. Eyes get a small glass-green sphere nested inside a brass torus bezel, rotated to face sideways on the head bone.

Ears are leather-colored slabs defined by six-point outlines hanging from the top of the skull on each side, and now I'm working out the winding key — a brass shaft and torus loop positioned at the hips on the spine bone.

For the chest, I'm figuring out where the front-facing surface is so I can place two gear mechanisms there using nearest-point hits, then building each gear as a small cylinder disc with teeth arranged in a ring around its edge, orienting the cylinder's axis to match the surface normal.

For rivets, I'm finding the nearest point on the body surface for each position and sticking a small sphere there with partial embedding, laid out in rows across z and y on both sides—around 36 total, staying well under the mesh limit. I'm also planning side plates as boxes placed via the same nearest-surface approach.

I want to add riveted plates on each side at a couple of z positions, oriented so the box thickness aligns with the surface normal, and then ring rivets around each plate's border using a helper that distributes items radially around a hit point—this gives a nice riveted-plate look without manually placing each rivet.

Rivets will stick up slightly above the plate surface which actually sells the riveted-plate look, so I'll place them along each plate's perimeter plus a couple in the middle rather than a full grid. Now I'm moving on to the tail — setting up a spiral path anchored near the rump, starting from a point on the body surface.

For the tail I'm building a four-segment chain along that spiral and sweeping it with a tapering radius in copper, which turns the helical centerline into a coiled, spring-like tube — a nice look. Next I'm figuring out where to anchor the neck chain off the chest/spine tip joint.

I'm laying out the neck as a short polyline from chest tip up toward the head, naming the three joints neck1, neck2, head, and sweeping it with a tapering brass radius for a smooth tapered neck. Then I'm working out how to place a collar torus so it sits perpendicular to the neck's tilt, computing the neck direction vector and figuring out the rotation needed to align the torus's default normal to that angle.

Still working through collar placement...

The tag placement near the chest should be fine visually. I'm now checking the export structure—need a meta object with name and description, plus the default export returning the builder's root. Then I'm working out the paw geometry and joint naming for front and hind legs, deciding on brass or copper coloring for the paw boxes.

Setting up module imports and color constants...

Building the hips, spine, and neck joint chains with their parent hierarchy...

Finishing the leg sweep and paw geometry, then checking joint parenting and chain naming for consistency before moving to construct the body loft shape.

Building head loft shape, neck sweep, and ear slabs...

Now I'm adding eyes with glass spheres and brass torus rims, a nose, and checking the key cylinder's position against the body's top station to make sure it sits correctly on the spine.

Next I'm writing the gear logic—placing a brass cylinder embedded in the body surface at a given point, then ringing copper box teeth around its rim at a slightly larger radius, checking that the teeth embed depth centers them properly on the gear's edge.

Then I'm picking specific coordinates for two gear instances on the chest, making sure their radii and positions keep them from overlapping too much on the body surface.

For the surface sampling, I'm reusing the computed body surface for nearest-point lookups rather than reconstructing it each time, caching it for efficiency. I'm also coding plate geometry for the sides of the body, using a thin box aligned to the surface normal at each sample point, colored copper, with rivets placed around the plate edges at varying z positions.

Working through rivet placement...

Checking the top rivet corner offset still falls within the body's side region, confirming placement is valid. I'm defining a small rivet-sticking helper that embeds copper spheres onto the nearest surface point, then moving on to building the tail as a tapered spiral chain swept with copper material.

I'm verifying the spiral parameters—checking that the rise along the tilted axis gives a reasonably sized coiled tail, and considering bumping the pitch up slightly for more visible curl. I confirm the chain-of-four tail joints samples correctly along that path.

Now I'm adding the collar torus and a small brass tag cylinder at the neck, checking that my rotation math correctly orients the torus's normal to tilt forward as intended, and that the tag cylinder's default Y-axis rotates to face front properly.

I'm deciding on color consistency—settling on hex string colors for small paint details like the tag and paws rather than named constants, and keeping copper for legs/tail and brass for structural parts like the neck and head.

I'm running through the full joint naming scheme to make sure there are no collisions—hips, spine, chest, neck, head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, paws, hips, knees, hocks, toes, and the auto-numbered tail joints—confirming the chain's default naming avoids any clashes with existing joint names.

I'm double-checking type compatibility across the API: bone references accepting joints or chains, sweep options accepting radius arrays and names, slab options accepting bone strings, and point inputs accepting plain number arrays—all looks consistent with the expected types.

I'm confirming paw placement at ground level so the rig stands properly, verifying segment counts and ring/surface calls use valid frame inputs, and now I'm finalizing the full code for output as a single block.
